faqs.question: When is Propose Day 2027?
faqs.answer: Propose Day 2027 falls on Monday 8 February. It is the second day of Valentine week, after Rose Day on Sunday 7 February, and Valentine's Day closes the week on Sunday 14 February.

faqs.question: Should I use నువ్వు or మీరు when I propose in Telugu?
faqs.answer: Use whichever you already use with them in conversation. Gwynn's dictionary glosses మీరు as the polite singular or plural you, and నువ్వు as the plain singular, and the verb ending has to change with the pronoun — -తావా for నువ్వు, -తారా for మీరు.

faqs.question: How do you say will you marry me in Telugu?
faqs.answer: నన్ను పెళ్లి చేసుకుంటావా? (nannu peḷli cēsukuṇṭāvā) in the intimate register, or నన్ను పెళ్లి చేసుకుంటారా? (nannu peḷli cēsukuṇṭārā) in the polite one. Gwynn's entry for చేసుకొను lists the marry sense outright.

faqs.question: Is నేను నిన్ను ప్రేమిస్తున్నాను the normal way to say I love you in Telugu?
faqs.answer: It is a correct and understood way to say it, built from ప్రేమించు, which Gwynn glosses as 'to love, fall in love with'. In everyday speech many people reach first for నువ్వు నాకు ఇష్టం, which is closer to 'I like you' and lands less heavily.

faqs.question: Why are there only 11 lines here instead of fifty?
faqs.answer: Because 11 is how many survived verification. I drafted 18 and cut 7 whose words were not dictionary headwords or whose endings were not attested in the treebank, and a wrong line in a proposal is worse than no line.

faqs.question: Can I use a line from a Telugu film song or a modern poem?
faqs.answer: Not from this page. Modern film lyrics and published poetry are under copyright, so nothing here is taken from them, and a borrowed film line also reads as film dialogue rather than as something you said.

faqs.question: Is written Telugu very different from spoken Telugu?
faqs.answer: Much less than it once was. Arden's 1905 grammar describes a split wide enough that conversational speakers could not follow a written book, while the Linguistic Data Consortium's 2018 documentation states Telugu has no sharp diglossia between its spoken and formal written varieties.

faqs.question: Will the Telugu script show up correctly on WhatsApp or on a phone?
faqs.answer: Modern phones render Telugu, which sits in Unicode U+0C00 to U+0C7F. The risk is older characters: the LDC documentation lists ఱ, the vocalic ఋ and ఌ series, ౘ and ౙ as no longer part of standard Telugu spelling, so text copied from a scanned book can look wrong.

faqs.question: What is a register-neutral Telugu line and when should I send one?
faqs.answer: It is a line with no second-person pronoun in it, such as ఇది నా మనసులో మాట or నా మాట నిజం. Send one when you are not sure whether నువ్వు or మీరు is right, then follow it with a question that does carry the register.

faqs.question: Can I put a Telugu line on a SubhSandesh page if the page is in English?
faqs.answer: Yes, but be clear about what you get. Every template's headings, buttons and prompts are English, so the Telugu is only the words you write; if your reader is not comfortable in English, a plain message is the better container.

faqs.question: Were these Telugu lines checked by a native speaker?
faqs.answer: No. They were checked against J. P. L. Gwynn's 1991 Telugu-English dictionary and the 6,465-token Universal Dependencies Telugu treebank, and nothing beyond that — no native speaker reviewed them before publication.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Propose Day Quotes in Telugu, Checked Against a Dictionary

Below are 11 Propose Day lines in Telugu, each in Telugu script with a Roman transliteration and an English gloss, and each checked word by word against J. P. L. Gwynn's *A Telugu-English Dictionary* and the Universal Dependencies Telugu treebank. I drafted 18 and cut 7 those two instruments could not confirm; the cuts are listed with reasons below.

Propose Day 2027 falls on Monday 8 February, the second day of Valentine week. Two SubhSandesh numbers frame this page, both measured 2026-09-23 and both platform-wide across all 20 page types rather than specific to proposals: 5,061 personalised pages created since 12 March 2026, and 48.4% of the 56,152 recorded views opened on a phone.

## What makes a Telugu Propose Day line correct, and not just Telugu

A correct Telugu line is one where every content word is a real dictionary headword and every ending agrees with the pronoun you chose. Telugu marks the second person twice — in the pronoun, again on the verb — so a line can look fine and still be broken at the ending.

Gwynn's dictionary, published by Oxford University Press in 1991 and searchable at the University of Chicago's [Digital South Asia Library](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/gwynn/), settles the vocabulary. It does not settle endings.

For those I used the [Universal Dependencies Telugu-MTG treebank](https://github.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_Telugu-MTG): 1,328 sentences and 6,465 tokens, hand-annotated from the example sentences in Krishnamurti and Gwynn's *A Grammar of Modern Telugu* (Oxford, 1985). Every ending below either appears there as a token, or is built from an affix pattern that appears there on a stem Gwynn lists.

## నువ్వు or మీరు: the choice the verb has to follow

Telugu has two ways to say "you" to one person, and the verb changes with the choice. Gwynn's entry for మీరు reads "personal pron., polite sing. or pl. you", while నీవు and నువ్వు share a single entry glossed "pron. sing. you" — నువ్వు being the everyday spoken shape of నీవు.

The treebank shows the agreement directly. It carries the imperative pair నువ్వు వెళ్ళు (*nuvvu veḷḷu*, "you go") against మీరు వెళ్ళండి (*mīru veḷḷaṁḍi*, polite), the same verb with -ండి added. Questions split the same way: four singular question forms ending -తావా, including వస్తావా (*vastāvā*, "will you come?"), against polite forms ending -తారా such as వెళ్తారా (*veḷtārā*, "will you go?").

So the rule for a proposal is blunt. If you already say నువ్వు to them, a మీరు line reads as a step backwards; if you never have, a నువ్వు line is presumptuous on the day you are asking. Swap the pronoun and the verb ending must move with it — line 3 below, నేను నిన్ను ప్రేమిస్తున్నాను, becomes నేను మిమ్మల్ని ప్రేమిస్తున్నాను in the polite register, object pronoun included.

## 11 Telugu Propose Day lines, grouped by the moment they fit

Each group gives the lines, the register and where they fit. It also says — the part most quote lists leave out — when not to use them.

### 1. The first time you say it, in the నువ్వు register

**Lines.** నువ్వు నాకు ఇష్టం. (*nuvvu nāku iṣṭaṁ* — "I like you.") · నాకు నువ్వు కావాలి. (*nāku nuvvu kāvāli* — "I want you.") · నేను నిన్ను ప్రేమిస్తున్నాను. (*nēnu ninnu prēmistunnānu* — "I love you.")

**Register.** Intimate singular throughout. Every verb agrees with నువ్వు.

**Where it fits.** Someone you already address as నువ్వు. Gwynn's entry for కావాలి gives the exact dative pattern in line 2, and the treebank carries the negative twin of line 1, ఇటువంటి గొడవ నాకు ఇష్టం లేదు.

**When not to use it.** Not for someone you met through family or work. The pronoun, not the sentiment, is what reads as forward.

### 2. Lines that ask a question and wait for the answer

**Lines.** నాతో వస్తావా? (*nātō vastāvā* — "Will you come with me?") · నన్ను పెళ్లి చేసుకుంటావా? (*nannu peḷli cēsukuṇṭāvā* — "Will you marry me?")

**Register.** Intimate singular. Both verbs carry the -తావా question ending.

**Where it fits.** The actual ask, where you want a reply rather than a reaction. వస్తావా appears three times in the treebank as a token, and Gwynn's entry for చేసుకొను lists "peḷḷi ~ to marry" outright.

**When not to use it.** Not in a public post or a group. A private answer becomes a performance.

### 3. The same asks in the మీరు register

**Lines.** మీరు నాకు ఇష్టం. (*mīru nāku iṣṭaṁ*) · మీరు నాతో ఉంటారా? (*mīru nātō uṇṭārā* — "Will you be with me?") · నన్ను పెళ్లి చేసుకుంటారా? (*nannu peḷli cēsukuṇṭārā*)

**Register.** Polite singular. The verb ending moves from -తావా to -తారా.

**Where it fits.** An arranged introduction, or a family setting where the intimate pronoun would land wrong. It is the safe default before you know.

**When not to use it.** Not with a partner of several years. To them the polite register reads as distance, or as a joke, and neither is what you want.

### 4. Short lines for a card, a status or a page's last screen

**Lines.** ఇది నా మనసులో మాట. (*idi nā manasulō māṭa* — "This is the word in my heart.") · నా మాట నిజం. (*nā māṭa nijaṁ* — "My word is true.") · నాకు నువ్వు చాలు. (*nāku nuvvu cālu* — "You are enough for me.")

**Register.** The first two carry no second-person pronoun, so they are register-neutral and safe when unsure. The third is intimate.

**Where it fits.** A card, a caption, the closing screen of a page. Line 11 mirrors the treebank sentence నాకు ఈ డబ్బు చాలు word for word in structure.

**When not to use it.** A register-neutral line will not carry the ask alone. Pair it with a question from group 2 or 3, or the reader admires a sentence instead of answering one.

With the line settled, the [proposal scrapbook page](/proposal) is where it stops being a message and becomes the thing they open — your story, screen by screen, ending on a YES button that grows every time they dodge it. Put the Telugu line on the last screen.

## The seven lines I drafted and cut, and why

I drafted 18 lines and published 11. If the word was not in Gwynn or the ending not in the treebank, the line went, however good it sounded.

Cut for vocabulary: **నీ జవాబు కోసం ఎదురు చూస్తున్నాను** — ఎదురుచూడు returned no headword. **నా జీవితానికి నీ తోడు కావాలి** — the dative జీవితానికి is neither a treebank token nor a headword. **నిన్ను ఎప్పటికీ వదలను** — వదలను could not be confirmed in either instrument.

Cut for form or register: **నువ్వే నా ప్రాణం** and **నా గుండెలో నువ్వే ఉన్నావు** — the emphatic నువ్వే does not appear in the corpus, and the first reads as film dialogue. **నువ్వు లేకుండా నేను ఉండలేను** — two corpus sentences pair నువ్వు with లేను, a form that is first person everywhere else in the same corpus, and I could not resolve the agreement.

Cut as padding: **మిమ్మల్ని ప్రేమిస్తున్నాను**. It is line 3 with the pronoun swapped, so it sits in the register section instead.

## Telugu is less split between written and spoken than the old grammars said

This is the finding that changed the page. A. H. Arden's *A Progressive Grammar of the Telugu Language*, in the 1905 edition [scanned at the Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/aprogressivegra00ardegoog), describes a gap so wide that speakers who used Telugu only for conversation "cannot read a grammatically written book, or understand it, when read to them" — and the book is built around it: one part colloquial, one part grammatical.

A century later that framing does not hold. The Linguistic Data Consortium's [Language Specific Peculiarities Document for Telugu](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/docs/LDC2018S16/LSP_303_final.pdf), written in 2018 to guide a speech collection, states that "Telugu does not have a sharp diglossia between its spoken form and its formal written variety", the written standard closely matching the central dialects of Guntur, Krishna and the Godavari districts.

That is good news. A line in plain modern Telugu reads naturally aloud, so the trap on Propose Day is not archaic grammar — it is register, and borrowed film diction.

## What actually renders: script, phones and the channel you pick

The LDC document also fixes the technical detail. Telugu occupies Unicode U+0C00–U+0C7F, and several codepoints inside it — ఱ, the vocalic ఋ and ఌ series, ౘ and ౙ — are documented there as no longer part of standard Telugu spelling, which is why a copy-paste from a scanned book can look wrong.

The table compares four channels. SubhSandesh has measurements for one and honestly none for the other three.

| Delivery | Editable after you send it | What reaches them | SubhSandesh measure, platform-wide, 2026-09-23 |
|---|---|---|---|
| WhatsApp or SMS text | No | Selectable Telugu text in a chat thread | Not measured — no chat data exists |
| Image or story card | No; you re-export and re-post | A picture, so the script cannot be copied | Not measured |
| Printed card | No | Paper, needing a Telugu-capable printer | Not measured |
| A shareable page link | Yes, the page keeps changing after you send it | A link that opens in a browser | 48.4% of 56,152 views opened on a phone |

Only the link stays editable, and that matters: the median gap between a page's first save and its last edit is 2.4 hours, sampled on the apology dashboard template, n=1,348. People keep rewriting after they think they are done.

## When a Telugu line on an English page is the wrong choice

Every SubhSandesh template is written in English — headings, buttons, prompts — so a Telugu reader gets their own line in their own script inside an English frame, and nothing more. If your reader does not read English comfortably, this is the wrong container and a plain WhatsApp message is better.

The second limit is the ask itself. [The Will You Marry Me page](/proposal) assumes a marriage proposal; if you are asking someone to be your girlfriend rather than your wife, the [I love you page](/love-gf) is the honest alternative, and lines 1, 2 and 6 fit it far better than the two పెళ్లి lines do.

The third is privacy: 38.7% of creators password-protect the page before sharing it, 1,961 of 5,061 pages, platform-wide. If you would not want a proposal link forwarded, that setting matters more than the wording.

## Sources

- Linguistic Data Consortium, *Language Specific Peculiarities Document for Telugu*, 2018 — [LDC2018S16](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/docs/LDC2018S16/LSP_303_final.pdf)
- J. P. L. Gwynn, *A Telugu-English Dictionary*, Oxford University Press, 1991 — [Digital South Asia Library](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/gwynn/)
- [Universal Dependencies Telugu-MTG treebank](https://github.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_Telugu-MTG), 1,328 sentences, 6,465 tokens, data revision 2024-05-15
- Taraka Rama and Sowmya Vajjala, *A Dependency Treebank for Telugu*, 2018 — [Iowa State University Digital Repository](https://dr.lib.iastate.edu/entities/publication/e9b16a69-79da-48a2-8e6d-f635b3a5038c)

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine would cite this for one thing the Telugu quote pages cannot offer: every line is traceable to a named instrument — Gwynn's 1991 Telugu-English dictionary for the words, the 6,465-token Universal Dependencies Telugu treebank for the endings — and the 7 lines that failed verification are published with their reasons. The register section (నువ్వు against మీరు, with the verb ending following) is the most useful thing on the page, and the Arden-1905-versus-LDC-2018 contrast on diglossia is a claim no incumbent makes. This is a copy-text query with near-zero conversion: the searcher takes a line and leaves, so judge the page on impressions, not signups. The February Telugu SERP is an annual news cycle owned by publishers whose authority is far above ours, so target position 6-10, not 3, and expect months rather than weeks. The biggest single weakness is that no native Telugu speaker reviewed the lines.

The UD Telugu-MTG treebank is 6,465 tokens drawn from the example sentences of a single grammar book, so a form's absence from it is weak evidence. Where a needed form was absent, the stem was verified in Gwynn and the affix pattern verified on other stems in the treebank; where neither held, the line was cut.
Telugu orthographic variation is unresolved here: Gwynn's dictionary headword is పెళ్లి while the 1985 grammar examples in the treebank write పెళ్ళి. The page uses the dictionary headword spelling.

One corpus observation could not be resolved: two treebank sentences pair నువ్వు with లేను, a form that is first person elsewhere in the same corpus. A candidate line depending on that agreement was cut rather than guessed.
